title: Is solar's growth finally slowing in the US?
gist: EIA data for the first seven months of 2026 show US electricity demand up only 2% (vs 3% a year earlier) despite data centers, and solar's absolute generation growth slowing to 39 TWh (22%) from 48 TWh amid federal hostility, yet wind and solar growth (55 TWh) still exceeded demand growth (51 TWh) while coal fell over 10%.

insights.claim: US grid electricity use rose only 2 percent year over year in the first seven months of 2026, versus 3 percent growth a year earlier, despite data centers and electrification from EVs and heat pumps.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Grid-demand growth is decelerating, tempering the most aggressive data-center power-demand narratives priced into utilities and IPPs.
insights.locator: The top line item is that

insights.claim: Grid demand growth may be muted because efficiency keeps improving and more data centers are generating their own power on-site, so their demand doesn't show up on the grid.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Behind-the-meter generation shifts data-center power spend from utilities toward on-site gas turbines and generation vendors.

insights.claim: US solar generation grew by 39 TWh (22 percent) in the first seven months of 2026 versus a 48 TWh increase in the same period of 2025, a considerable slowdown in absolute additions after 30%+ growth rates.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A drop in absolute solar additions, not just percentage growth, is a negative volume signal for US solar developers and installers.

insights.claim: The federal government's hostility to renewables and removal of incentives may be slowing solar's expansion even though solar is the cheapest way to meet rising demand.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Policy headwinds are showing up in deployment data; policy risk remains the key driver for US solar equities.

insights.claim: Small-scale solar such as rooftop grew over 12 percent year over year, slower than utility-scale.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Residential solar is lagging utility-scale growth.

insights.claim: Solar produced 72 percent as much electricity as coal in the first seven months of 2026, with coal generation down a bit over 10 percent year over year despite the Trump administration's efforts to support coal.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Coal's structural decline continues regardless of federal policy support.

insights.claim: Year over year, hydro rose 9 percent, wind 6 percent, and nuclear and natural gas each less than 2 percent.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Gas generation is roughly flat, limiting incremental power-sector gas demand growth.

insights.claim: Wind and solar grew 55 TWh while grid demand rose 51 TWh in the first seven months of 2026, meaning renewable growth alone covered all of the increase in electricity use.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Incremental demand is being met by renewables, not fossil fuels, capping growth for gas and coal generators.

insights.claim: Wind and solar now supply 21 percent of US electricity, renewables including hydro 27 percent, and all non-carbon sources including nuclear 45 percent, versus the EU at about 30 percent wind and solar and 65 percent emissions-free.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: US decarbonization trails the EU, leaving runway for further renewable share gains.

insights.claim: Two large East Coast offshore wind projects, including a 2.6 GW project off Virginia, will be completed, but they are likely the last until the 2030s because the Trump administration has paid developers to stop building similar projects.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: US offshore wind pipeline is effectively frozen after current projects; onshore wind in the Midwest and Plains continues.

insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Falling costs are widening the geographic market for solar-plus-storage, supporting battery storage suppliers.
